references.text: The tax collector beat his breast in sorrow and humility – the same expression (τύπτοντες τὰ στήθη) is used here in [ref:Luk 18:13|Luke 18:13] to describe beating one's breast as a sign of grief and repentance, just as the crowd does after witnessing Jesus' death.
In [ref:Luk 23:35|Luke 23:35], the people stand watching (θεωροῦντες) the crucifixion. The same crowd that were spectators (θεωρίαν) to these events now returns home in sorrow, beating their breasts.

The officer's reaction in [ref:Luk 23:47|Luke 23:47], where he praises God and declares Jesus righteous, precedes the crowd's response in verse 48 – both testify that what happened at the cross evoked deep realization among the onlookers.

In [ref:Luk 23:49|Luke 23:49], those who knew Jesus and the women who had followed him from Galilee are described as standing and watching. The crowd in verse 48 leaves the place, but Jesus' closest followers remain standing.

Zechariah's prophecy in [ref:Sak 12:10-14|Zechariah 12:10-14] that the people will look on him whom they have pierced and mourn has a thematic parallel to the crowd's grief and repentance as they witness Jesus' death and beat their breasts.

In [ref:Apg 2:37|Acts 2:37], the listeners were "pierced in the heart" (κατενύγησαν τὴν καρδίαν) after Peter's sermon on how they crucified Jesus. The crowd's reaction at the cross in Luke 23:48 can be seen as a precursor to this deeper repentance.

Isaiah's suffering servant song in [ref:Jes 53:3-5|Isaiah 53:3-5] describes him as despised and full of sorrow, pierced for our transgressions. The crowd's sorrowful response in Luke 23:48 reflects a beginning realization of what has happened to the innocent one.

The travelers on the road to Emmaus in [ref:Luk 24:19-20|Luke 24:19-20] summarize the events: how the chief priests and rulers handed Jesus over to be condemned to death and crucified him. This confirms the collective awareness of "what had happened" (τὰ γενόμενα) that the crowd reacted to in 23:48.
